title: How widely jazz was accepted in New Orleans, and by whom
summary: He thinks most New Orleanians accepted jazz, especially dancers and party-goers, and that devotees were truly enthused. He cannot say what others thought thirty years ago.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: I can give you. I just feel confident that if my memory is correct, there were times where I, when I did, looked down my nose in jazz. And you said a great number of people that did. I think that there were... I think there were many that did. Would you say a majority of New Orleans? No, I'd say the majority accepted it. I'd say the majority accepted it and recognized it as... Well, you see, here's the point. If a person was a dancer and a dancegoer and a party man, and he'd hear it at the party and hear it to dances, he had to be part of his experience. I didn't go in for that much. And as a consequence, my experience was less limited

than someone else's. And your liking or disliking for something is frequently predicated upon your experience. Yes, sir. So not having had such an experience. You see what I mean? Yes, sir. Well, taking all that for granted, then, what did you... Did you know as Oswald now people were greatly enthused over it? I wouldn't say that I knew a great number that were enthused over it, but I would certainly say that those who enthused over it actually really enthused over it. You know what I mean? They were devotees, devotees. Yes, sir. They were devotees. Well, among these people, you said that

most of the people that did like it were people who went to dance. Did they just think of it as a form of entertainment, just music? You were asking me to project myself back 30 years into somebody's mind that I didn't have been
